extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, journalists, and media critics interested in media theory and news bias
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the Propaganda Model's filters and related evaluative criteria to assess how news is selected, framed, and constrained by institutional forces (sources, flak, ideology, resources, expert selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: SOURCING MASS-MEDIA NEWS: THE THIRD FILTER
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass media are drawn into a symbiotic relationship with powerful sources of information by economic necessity and reciprocity of interest; the media need a steady, reliable flow of the raw material of news and therefore concentrate resources where significant news often occurs (White House, Pentagon, State Department, city hall, police, corporations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of daily news demands and schedules, news organizations depend on regular, routinized sources; this creates privileged access for large bureaucracies and corporations that can reliably supply material. Examples: Washington beats, business beats; Fishman's 'principle of bureaucratic affinity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of bureaucratic affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Only other bureaucracies can satisfy the input needs of a news bureaucracy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworkers are predisposed to treat bureaucratic accounts as factual because officials are seen as 'authorized knowers.' This moral division of labor leads reporters to accept officials' claims as presumptively credible rather than fully investigating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for 'credible' official sources to preserve objectivity and reduce cost/liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass media favor material that can be portrayed as presumptively accurate to maintain the image of objectivity and to protect from criticisms of bias or libel suits; taking information from credible sources reduces investigative expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This incentive structure makes costly investigative reporting less likely, while stories from prima facie credible sources are preferred. Anti-pattern: privileging official statements without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/resource asymmetry of public-information operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large government agencies and corporations run vast public-information operations (e.g., the Pentagon's thousands of employees, hundreds of millions of dollars, extensive press products) that dwarf the resources of dissenting individuals and nonprofit organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical examples illustrate the imbalance (Pentagon periodicals, Air Force outreach vs AFSC/NCC budgets). The result: the large players can dominate media supply and attention by sheer volume and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate and trade-association resources as privileged news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the corporate sector has resources to produce public information and propaganda on the scale of large government bodies; many corporations and trade associations maintain large communications budgets, publications, and broadcast activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: U.S. Chamber of Commerce budgets and media products; corporate political advertising and direct-mail campaigns. These resources enable corporations to consolidate preeminence as news sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of ready-to-use materials and the subsidy effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful sources provide the media with facilities to gather, advance copies of speeches and reports, scheduled press conferences, press releases in usable language, and carefully organized 'photo opportunity' sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces media costs of acquiring and producing news (a subsidy) and thereby increases the likelihood media will use material from such sources. Examples: press release services, media orientation flights, photo ops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged/routine sources vs. non-routine sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Large entities that supply continuous, scheduled material become 'routine' news sources with privileged access to the gates; non-routine sources must struggle for access and may be ignored by gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine sources gain trusted status; non-routine or dissenting voices face higher sourcing costs and less credibility, making their stories less likely to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of the media by inundation (flooding with 'facts')
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful sources manage the media by inundating them with stories to foist particular lines or to chase unwanted stories off the front page or out of the media altogether; historically associated with coordinated propaganda efforts (e.g., Committee on Public Information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include massive release of 'facts' and scheduled leaks/press events to set the agenda. Example: using many stories to frame Nicaragua as illicitly supplying arms or to divert attention from other events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-opting the experts / creating the needed body of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias may be structured by co-opting experts: putting them on payrolls as consultants, funding their research, organizing think tanks that hire them and help disseminate their messages so that commonly held opinions gain authoritative voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include buying academic reputations (Powell memo), funding think tanks, and disseminating funded intellectuals' work to the press. Feulner's analogy: selling and reselling a product (ideas) to keep it fresh in the public mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture and promotion of 'experts' by the media
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass media themselves provide 'experts' who echo official views; by giving exposure, the media confer status on purveyors of preferred views (e.g., journalists-authors, defectors, ex-radicals turned establishment commentators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Reader's Digest promoting Barron and Sterling; Time/ABC/NYT featuring Arkady Shevchenko despite tarnished credentials; ex-radicals elevated after changing stance. The media's selection confers authority and supplies obvious candidates for commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: FLAK AND THE ENFORCERS: THE FOURTH FILTER
rubrics_metrics.description: "Flak" = negative responses to a media statement or program (letters, phone calls, petitions, lawsuits, speeches, bills, etc.); flak can be organized or individual and, when produced at scale or by powerful actors, can be uncomfortable and costly to media organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include internal defense, legislative or legal exposure, and withdrawn advertising. Historical examples: McCarthy-era boycotts and blacklisting; modern threats from the White House, FCC requests, or corporate advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized flak producers and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions have been established to produce flak—monitoring groups, legal foundations, think tanks and advocacy organizations aimed at harassing or disciplining the media (e.g., American Legal Foundation, Capital Legal Foundation, Media Institute, Center for Media and Public Affairs, Accuracy in Media (AIM), Freedom House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These organizations may specialize in complaints (Fairness Doctrine), libel suits, monitoring studies, and public pressure campaigns. Funding and elite backing give them power to condition media behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser pressure and economic boycotts as flak
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers may withdraw patronage or threaten boycotts in response to media content; television advertising in consumer goods is particularly vulnerable to organized boycotts, creating a deterrent against offending constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertiser pressure is both a direct and indirect form of flak, influencing programming choices and contributing to self-censorship within media organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticommunism as a control mechanism (ideological filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideology of anticommunism acts as a final filter: it is a dominant first principle that helps mobilize the populace, fragments the left, and can be used against anyone advocating policies that threaten property interests; the concept is sufficiently fuzzy to be widely applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticommunist framing suspends normal evidentiary demands, elevates certain 'experts' (defectors, ideologues), and causes liberal actors to demonstrate anti-Communist credentials, often aligning them with reactionary policies. Examples: selective attention to dissidents, willingness to accept unreliable defectors as authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichotomization of victims and selection for propaganda campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The filters produce a natural dichotomization of 'worthy' and 'unworthy' victims; issues that are useful to elite interests become the focus of sustained propaganda campaigns, while equally severe abuses that conflict with elite interests are ignored or marginalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: contrast between attention to Polish trade-union repression (worthy) and Turkish torture or Indonesian massacres (unworthy), KAL 007 coverage vs. Libyan civilian airliner, and the use of stories when they serve a 'useful purpose' (Gwertzman/NYT quote). Propaganda campaigns may be initiated by government, media firms, or both, and require media collaboration.
